summary: RADIUM is an open-source tool that searches the entire Earth for the best places to rehearse missions to the Moon and Mars. It opens with one question, "What do you want to find out?", and three clicks later you are looking at a side-by-side Earth match. Choose any point on a 3D Moon or Mars and what you want to test there (rover driving, ice drilling, field geology, dust on solar panels, or life detection), and RADIUM scores all 341,042 land areas on Earth against it in about a second. It measures terrain, rock chemistry, ground ice, dryness, temperature, and airborne dust the same way on all three worlds, using 18 public datasets from NASA and partner agencies. A separate score grades Moon and Mars locations for a permanent base or a landing. Every match shows what lines up, what doesn't, and what Earth can never reproduce, such as gravity, air pressure, and radiation. For Mons Mouton, a mountain in one of NASA's Artemis landing regions, RADIUM's best Earth match is the dry Andean foothills near Pachacámac, southeast of Lima, at grade A(0.81), with matching slope and roughness and a rock type close to the lunar highlands, though the temperature differs greatly. It is built to serve mission planners and first-time explorers alike.
details:
The Problem

Space agencies test rovers, drills, instruments and field procedures at terrestrial analog sites before flying them. The Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater and Death Valley are well-known examples. The right site depends on where the mission is going and what is being tested, though. A place that resembles Martian terrain for a rover trial may be a poor place to practice drilling into ground ice. Choosing a site usually means reading field studies of individual locations one at a time. We wanted to see whether NASA and partner-agency datasets could be used to compare every land area on Earth against one specific point on the Moon or Mars, for one specific kind of test.

What It Does

RADIUM has two separate functions.

The first evaluates locations on the Moon or Mars for a mission. The user picks a permanent lunar base, a robotic Mars landing or a human Mars mission, then sets how much ice access, sunlight, terrain safety, temperature and contact with Earth should count. Every location receives a grade from A to F. Optional hard limits, such as ground too steep to build on, remove locations outright.

The second starts from one point on the Moon or Mars and a test purpose: rover driving, ice drilling, field geology, dust on solar panels, or life detection. RADIUM compares that point with all 341,042 land areas on Earth, ranks the closest matches, and shows which measurements agree and which do not.

We kept these as two separate scores because they answer different questions. A location on Earth can be useful for testing equipment bound for a site that would be a poor place to land, and a good landing site may have no close counterpart on Earth. A combined number would hide both cases. The app opens by asking what the user wants to find out, and three steps (site, test, results) lead to a side-by-side comparison. Changing a weight re-ranks the list and shows which places moved.

How a Match Is Measured

Terrain. Elevation comes from different instruments on each world: LOLA on the Moon, MOLA on Mars, and NOAA's ETOPO 2022 on Earth. Slopes measured over different distances describe different features, so they cannot be compared directly. We used grids of about 1.9 km per pixel for all three and calculated every terrain value over the same 3.7 km baseline, correcting the east-west step for latitude so the distance stays constant away from the equator. For each area we record the typical slope, the slope of the steepest 10% of the ground, and surface roughness.

Geology. Earth rock types come from the Global Lithological Map, which sorts land into sixteen classes. On the Moon, Lunar Prospector iron oxide measurements separate iron-rich basalt plains from feldspar-rich highland rock, and we match that mix against the Earth classes. The map groups anorthosite with gabbro, so highland matches are capped below a perfect score. For Mars we start from the basaltic crust mapped across most of the planet, then shift the comparison toward loose sediment where low thermal inertia indicates a dust mantle, and toward salt deposits where Mars Odyssey measures elevated chlorine.

Ice and climate. Hydrogen on its own does not mean ice. On Mars, shallow ground ice is stable only where the annual mean surface temperature is about 198 K or colder, so Odyssey hydrogen counts as ice evidence only inside that zone. In warmer ground it is more likely bound in hydrated minerals. On the Moon we combine distance to permanently shadowed craters, hydrogen abundance, and Diviner's estimate of where ice could stay stable within the top meter. On Earth, MODIS vegetation data and NASA POWER rainfall measure how bare and dry each area is. Mars comparisons also include ground temperature and airborne dust.

Ranking. The weights depend on the test. Rover driving puts half its weight on terrain, while life detection leans on dryness, cold and ice. Earth areas missing too much of the needed data are not ranked, because a score built on one or two measurements would look more precise than it is. The top results are kept at least 500 km apart, so the list shows different regions instead of neighboring cells from the same area.

Limits. Gravity, atmospheric pressure and radiation are left out of the similarity score. Every Earth site differs from the Moon or Mars on these in roughly the same way, so scoring them would make the results misleading without helping tell sites apart. Each comparison reports them separately with numbers, including published radiation measurements of about 0.64 mSv/day at Gale crater and 1.37 mSv/day on the Moon, against about 2.4 mSv/year of background radiation on Earth, along with the kind of facility needed to make up each difference.

What We Found

For Jezero crater, the highest-ranked Earth areas for life-detection testing are in the Chilean Andes, on the Mongolian Plateau and in the Atacama Desert. The list of known analog sites is only used to label results, and a test confirms that removing it changes no score, so the Atacama ranked highly from the measurements alone. That does not validate the whole model, but it agrees with decades of Mars research done there.

For the Apollo 11 region, the best field-geology matches are in Saudi Arabia and Jordan, both scoring 0.84. Meteor Crater scores 0.72 for the same target. This reflects the weights for that purpose, which emphasize rock type and bare ground.

For ice drilling at Arcadia Planitia on Mars, no Earth location earns an A. The best score is 0.79, in East Antarctica, so even the closest Earth analog for that site has clear gaps.

On the mission side, only one of 355,896 lunar locations grades A for a permanent base under the default weights, near the north pole. Few places score well on ice access, sunlight and buildable terrain at the same time. Different weights would produce a different answer.

We checked the model against published values. Our lunar slopes correlate with NASA's LOLA slope product at 0.94. The best-lit point near the lunar south pole falls where published illumination studies place it. MOLA elevations at eight Mars landing sites agree within 0.6 km, and the default Mars landing ranking places Gale, Meridiani and Oxia Planum among its top regions. The project has 127 automated tests.

Two problems in the source data came up during these checks. One Diviner polar table correlated with LOLA topography at only 0.11. After reversing its longitudes the correlation rose to 0.999, and we confirmed the orientation using 21 IAU crater positions. Separately, MODIS land cover labeled bright salt flats such as Bonneville and Lop Nur as permanent snow, even where mean ground temperatures are above 10 °C. We reassigned those 122 cells before running the final comparisons.

Impact

A mission team can use RADIUM to build a shortlist of Earth test sites for a specific target and test, along with the conditions each site cannot simulate, so they know which parts of a test will need a vacuum chamber or a reduced-gravity setup. Researchers can review the datasets, weights and rules, and rebuild every grid from the original sources using the code on GitHub. Students can use Near Me to find studied analog sites close to home. From Las Vegas, for example, the Pisgah Lava Field, where researchers have tested thermal imaging for cave detection, is about 190 km away. RADIUM works at a scale of 2 to 30 km per cell, so it is a screening tool, not a way to certify a landing site.

What Makes It Creative

Mission suitability and analog similarity stay separate, and the ranking changes when the user's priorities change. Every match comes with a one-line explanation of why it ranks where it does, and the conditions Earth cannot reproduce are reported next to the score. Terrain is measured the same way on three worlds with different instruments, which is what makes a cross-planet comparison possible. We also wanted the same tool to work for someone new to planetary science and for a specialist. A first-time user can follow the three-step flow, watch a 20-second example that runs the real controls, and see short tips the first time they are needed. A specialist can see measured values with units and sources, uncertainty ranges where the data provide them, adjustable weights, data exports and a printable test plan.

Tools

The data pipeline and scoring service are written in Python (NumPy, SciPy, FastAPI). The website uses TypeScript and React, with CesiumJS for the 3D globes and MapLibre for the Earth map, and it is hosted on Vercel with the code on GitHub. Before writing any code we used Google Docs to research analog sites and decide which characteristics should count in a comparison. We then built several prototypes and combined the strongest parts. AI coding assistants wrote much of the code and proposed some default weights and thresholds, working from our specification; we set the scientific rules and the design, and reviewed the results. Details are in our AI-use disclosure.
